title: Due-Process Voluntariness of Confessions

case_set.caption: Brown v. Mississippi
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: convictions resting 'solely upon confessions shown to have been extorted by officers of the State by brutality and violence' are inconsistent with Fourteenth Amendment due process.

case_set.caption: Chambers v. Florida
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'five days of continued questioning' of incommunicado prisoners held to show 'compulsion was applied' — protracted secret interrogation voids the convictions.

case_set.caption: Ashcraft v. Tennessee
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 36 hours of incommunicado relay questioning without sleep is 'so inherently coercive that its very existence is irreconcilable with the possession of mental freedom.'

case_set.caption: Spano v. New York
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'petitioner's will was overborne by official pressure, fatigue and sympathy falsely aroused' (childhood-'false friend' ploy), 'after considering all the facts' — totality method.

case_set.caption: Rogers v. Richmond
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: voluntariness must be judged 'with complete disregard of whether or not petitioner in fact spoke the truth'; a standard weighing 'probable truth or falsity' is impermissible under due process.

case_set.caption: Lynumn v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: confession after police threatened she could 'get 10 years and the children could be taken away' is 'not voluntary, but coerced'; 'the question in each case is whether the defendant's will was overborne.'

case_set.caption: Townsend v. Sain
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: confession elicited after injection of hyoscine, 'claimed... to have the properties of a truth serum,' with officer conditioning medical aid on 'cooperation' — involuntariness from drug-induced questioning.

case_set.caption: Haynes v. Washington
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: confession 'obtained under a totality of circumstances evidencing an involuntary written admission of guilt' — incommunicado detention and the 'unfair and inherently coercive context' defeat voluntariness.

case_set.caption: Lego v. Twomey
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: judge may admit a confession on finding it 'voluntary by a preponderance of the evidence'; rejects arguments for a higher burden or separate jury voluntariness verdict.

case_set.caption: Schneckloth v. Bustamonte
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: consent-search voluntariness is 'a question of fact to be determined from the totality of all the circumstances' — expressly borrowing the confession-voluntariness standard.

case_set.caption: Mincey v. Arizona
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: statements taken from a wounded, hospitalized suspect held involuntary and inadmissible even where offered only 'to impeach his credibility' — involuntary statements are unusable for any purpose.

case_set.caption: Colorado v. Connelly
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'coercive police activity is a necessary predicate to the finding that a confession is not voluntary' — the 'voice of God' command-hallucination confession was not involuntary absent state overreaching.

case_set.caption: Arizona v. Fulminante
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'a credible threat of physical violence' suffices for coercion ('a finding of coercion need not depend upon actual violence'), and admission of a coerced confession is reviewed for harmless error.

case_set.caption: Chavez v. Martinez
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: coercive questioning of Martinez, whose answers 'were never used against him in any criminal proceeding,' framed the holding that the self-incrimination guarantee is a trial-use right — cabining civil enforcement of voluntariness.

case_set.caption: Bram v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Nineteenth-century self-incrimination voluntariness anchor (confession must not be extracted by threats or promises); no lake record/cached text — basis from lane knowledge only.

case_set.caption: Payne v. Arkansas
case_set.one_line_basis: Coerced-confession reversal (threat of mob violence); admission of a coerced confession vitiates the judgment; no lake record/cached text.

case_set.caption: Leyra v. Denno
case_set.one_line_basis: Psychiatrist-as-interrogator deception held coercive; no lake record/cached text.

case_set.caption: Blackburn v. Alabama
case_set.one_line_basis: Confession of an insane suspect held involuntary — mental condition weighed pre-Connelly; no lake record/cached text.

case_set.caption: Culombe v. Connecticut
case_set.one_line_basis: Frankfurter's canonical totality formulation (will overborne / capacity for self-determination critically impaired); no lake record/cached text.

case_set.caption: Jackson v. Denno
case_set.one_line_basis: Procedural companion — defendant entitled to a reliable pretrial judicial determination of voluntariness; no lake record/cached text.

case_set.caption: Miller v. Fenton
case_set.one_line_basis: Voluntariness is a legal question subject to independent federal review on habeas; no lake record/cached text.

negative_notes: No SCOTUS holding that police deception or false promises alone render a confession involuntary — trickery remains one totality factor (Frazier v. Cupp, not in lake, would be the cite).

Post-Connelly, personal characteristics (mental illness, intoxication) matter only as they bear on susceptibility to actual police coercion; there is no free-standing reliability screen under due process (Connelly text: rejecting involuntariness absent police overreaching).
No split signal derived: the SCOTUS voluntariness line is internally consistent; disputes are application-level (totality weighing), not rule-level.

title: Miranda: Waiver and Invocation

case_set.caption: Miranda v. Arizona
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: rights may be waived 'provided the waiver is made voluntarily, knowingly and intelligently'; 'a heavy burden rests on the government' to prove waiver; invocation 'in any manner and at any stage' cuts off questioning.

case_set.caption: Michigan v. Mosley
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: invocation of silence turns on whether the 'right to cut off questioning' was 'scrupulously honored' — resumption after a significant interval on a different crime with fresh warnings permitted.

case_set.caption: North Carolina v. Butler
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: express waiver 'is not inevitably either necessary or sufficient'; silence 'coupled with an understanding of his rights and a course of conduct indicating waiver' can establish waiver.

case_set.caption: Fare v. Michael C.
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: a juvenile's request for his probation officer is not a per se invocation; waiver and invocation are assessed under the totality of the circumstances.

case_set.caption: Edwards v. Arizona
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: once counsel is invoked, no interrogation 'unless the accused himself initiates further communication, exchanges, or conversations with the police.'

case_set.caption: Oregon v. Bradshaw
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'initiation' means statements representing 'a desire... to open up a more generalized discussion relating directly or indirectly to the investigation,' not routine custodial inquiries.

case_set.caption: Smith v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: rejects the Illinois court's use of 'post-request responses' to render an initial request for counsel 'ambiguous' — clarity is judged at the moment of the request.

case_set.caption: Oregon v. Elstad
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'a subsequent administration of Miranda warnings to a suspect who has given a voluntary but unwarned statement' ordinarily suffices — no 'fruit of the poisonous tree' presumption of compulsion.

case_set.caption: Moran v. Burbine
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'Events occurring outside of the presence of the suspect and entirely unknown to him' (police failure to tell him of his attorney's efforts) 'can have no bearing on the capacity to comprehend and knowingly relinquish' the rights.

case_set.caption: Connecticut v. Barrett
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: an invocation limited to 'counsel before making a written statement' does not bar use of the suspect's oral statement — invocations are read for their ordinary, limited meaning.

case_set.caption: Colorado v. Spring
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'mere silence by law enforcement officials as to the subject matter of an interrogation' is not trickery that invalidates a waiver — awareness of all possible topics is not required.

case_set.caption: Colorado v. Connelly
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'the State need prove waiver only by a preponderance of the evidence,' and waiver involuntariness requires police coercion, not free-standing mental incapacity.

case_set.caption: Arizona v. Roberson
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: Edwards applies to 'police-initiated interrogation following a suspect's request for counsel... in the context of a separate investigation' — emphasizing 'the virtues of a bright-line rule.'

case_set.caption: Minnick v. Mississippi
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: once counsel is requested, interrogation without counsel present is barred even after the suspect has consulted his lawyer — Edwards protection does not lapse on consultation.

case_set.caption: McNeil v. Wisconsin
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'the Sixth Amendment right... is offense specific'; invoking counsel at a judicial proceeding on a charged offense does not invoke the Miranda-Edwards counsel right for other investigations.

case_set.caption: Davis v. United States (1994)
case_set.one_line_basis: Post-waiver invocation of counsel must be unambiguous; 'maybe I should talk to a lawyer' insufficient. Cached text is an 88-byte stub, so grounded via Berghuis v. Thompkins text quoting Davis: a suspect 'must do so unambiguously,' and if the statement 'is ambiguous or equivocal... police are not required to end the interrogation.'

case_set.caption: Berghuis v. Thompkins
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: invocation of silence must be unambiguous (extending Davis), and 'a Miranda warning... [followed by] an uncoerced statement' with understanding of the rights establishes an implied waiver.

case_set.caption: Maryland v. Shatzer
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'a break in custody ends the presumption of involuntariness established in Edwards'; the Court fixes '14 days' as the period that dissipates residual coercion.

case_set.caption: Missouri v. Seibert
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: the 'question-first' protocol fails because a 'midstream recitation of warnings after interrogation and unwarned confession could not effectively comply with Miranda's constitutional requirement.'

case_set.caption: United States v. Patane
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: whether Miranda 'requires suppression of the physical fruits of the suspect's unwarned but voluntary statements' — answered no (the Glock located through the unwarned statement was admissible).

case_set.caption: Montejo v. Louisiana
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'Michigan v. Jackson should be and now is overruled' — no automatic Sixth Amendment bar on police-initiated interrogation after counsel is appointed; Edwards/Miranda protections remain the safeguard.

case_set.caption: Michigan v. Tucker
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: testimony of a witness located through un-Mirandized questioning need not be excluded — the violation was of 'the prophylactic rules developed to protect' the right, not the privilege itself.

case_set.caption: Harris v. New York
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: statements taken without compliance with Miranda may be used 'to impeach his credibility' — the shield is not 'a license to use perjury.'

case_set.caption: Doyle v. Ohio
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'use of the defendant's post-arrest silence' after Miranda warnings to impeach 'violates due process' — the warnings carry an implicit assurance silence will not be penalized.

case_set.caption: Tague v. Louisiana
case_set.one_line_basis: Per curiam: no waiver where the State offered no evidence the suspect understood the rights read to him; no lake record/cached text.

case_set.caption: Oregon v. Hass
case_set.one_line_basis: Statements taken after an ignored counsel request usable for impeachment (Harris extension); no lake record/cached text.

title: Miranda and Custodial Interrogation

case_set.caption: Miranda v. Arizona
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'custodial interrogation' means 'questioning initiated by law enforcement officers after a person has been taken into custody or otherwise deprived of his freedom of action in any significant way'; warnings are the required safeguard.

case_set.caption: Escobedo v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: where investigation 'has begun to focus on a particular suspect' in custody who has 'requested and been denied' counsel, statements are inadmissible — the pre-Miranda focus test the later cases confine.

case_set.caption: Mathis v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: IRS questioning about 'claims for tax refunds' of a man imprisoned on other matters required warnings — custody on an unrelated offense is still custody.

case_set.caption: Orozco v. Texas
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'four police officers' questioning petitioner in his boardinghouse bedroom at 4 a.m. while 'under arrest and not free to leave' was custodial — custody is not limited to the stationhouse.

case_set.caption: Beckwith v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: rejects 'focus' of a criminal tax investigation as the trigger; 'noncustodial interrogation' by IRS agents in a private home did not require warnings.

case_set.caption: Oregon v. Mathiason
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: suspect who 'came voluntarily to the police station,' was told he was not under arrest, and 'did in fact leave... without hindrance' was not in custody; a 'coercive environment' alone does not trigger Miranda.

case_set.caption: Rhode Island v. Innis
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: interrogation covers 'express questioning or its functional equivalent' — words or actions 'the police should know are reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response.'

case_set.caption: California v. Prysock
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: warnings need no rigid formula where police 'fully conveyed' the rights — substance over incantation.

case_set.caption: California v. Beheler
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: custody question is whether there was 'formal arrest or restraint on freedom of movement' of the degree associated with formal arrest — 'coercive environment' framing again rejected.

case_set.caption: Berkemer v. McCarty
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: Miranda applies to 'a misdemeanor traffic offense,' but 'roadside questioning of a motorist detained pursuant to a traffic stop' is ordinarily not custodial interrogation.

case_set.caption: New York v. Quarles
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'overriding considerations of public safety justify the officer's failure to provide Miranda warnings before he asked questions devoted to locating the abandoned weapon' — objective, 'kaleidoscopic'-situation exception.

case_set.caption: Arizona v. Mauro
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: allowing the suspect 'to speak with his wife in the presence of a police officer' was not the 'functional equivalent' of interrogation under Innis.

case_set.caption: Duckworth v. Eagan
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: warnings including 'if and when you go to court' language upheld against the Seventh Circuit — adequacy judged by whether warnings as a whole convey the Miranda rights.

case_set.caption: Illinois v. Perkins
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'undercover government agent... placed in the cell' triggers no warnings — 'the essential ingredients of a police-dominated atmosphere and compulsion are not present' when the suspect thinks he is talking to an inmate.

case_set.caption: Pennsylvania v. Muniz
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: recognizes a 'routine booking question' exception, while the 'sixth birthday' question was testimonial and inadmissible without warnings; slurred speech is non-testimonial physical evidence.

case_set.caption: Stansbury v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'the initial determination of custody depends on the objective circumstances of the interrogation, not on the subjective views harbored by either the interrogating officers or the person being questioned.'

case_set.caption: Thompson v. Keohane
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: whether a suspect is 'in custody' is 'a mixed question of law and fact qualifying for independent review' — framed by the reasonable-person free-to-leave inquiry.

case_set.caption: Dickerson v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: Miranda 'announced a constitutional rule,' and 'Congress may not legislatively supersede our decisions interpreting and applying the Constitution' — §3501 invalid.

case_set.caption: Yarborough v. Alvarado
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: state court reasonably applied the objective 'reasonable person... at liberty to leave' custody test without weighing the suspect's age or experience (AEDPA posture).

case_set.caption: J. D. B. v. North Carolina
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'the age of a child subjected to police questioning is relevant to the custody analysis of Miranda' — an objective characteristic officers can perceive.

case_set.caption: Howes v. Fields
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: precedent does not 'clearly establish' a categorical rule that questioning a prisoner in private about outside events is custodial; 'imprisonment alone' does not constitute Miranda custody.

case_set.caption: Salinas v. Texas
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: a suspect 'without being placed in custody or receiving Miranda warnings' who 'voluntarily answered' questions must 'expressly invoke the privilege' — noncustodial silence is not self-executing.

case_set.caption: Chavez v. Martinez
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: coercive questioning without use of the statements in a criminal case supported no §1983 self-incrimination claim — the Miranda/5A core is a trial right.

case_set.caption: Vega v. Tekoh
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'a violation of the Miranda rules does not provide' a basis for §1983 damages — Miranda violations are not themselves completed constitutional violations for civil suit.

case_set.caption: Florida v. Powell
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: warnings suffice if 'the totality of the warning reasonably conveyed' the right to counsel's presence — 'right to talk to a lawyer before answering' plus 'at any time' language upheld.

case_set.caption: Estelle v. Smith
case_set.one_line_basis: Court-ordered psychiatric interview of a charged defendant used at capital sentencing required warnings; no lake record/cached text.

case_set.caption: Minnesota v. Murphy
case_set.one_line_basis: Probation interview held noncustodial; obligation to appear and answer truthfully did not create Miranda custody; no lake record/cached text.

title: Public-Employee Compelled Statements (Garrity)

case_set.caption: Garrity v. New Jersey
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: officers' statements 'were coerced... by reason of the fact that, if they refused to answer, they could lose their positions with the police department' — job-forfeiture threat makes the statements inadmissible in criminal proceedings.

case_set.caption: Gardner v. Broderick
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: patrolman 'discharged solely for' refusing to 'waive his privilege against self-incrimination' before a grand jury — the State may not condition public employment on a waiver of the privilege.

case_set.caption: Lefkowitz v. Turley
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: statutes cancelling contracts and disqualifying 'a contractor [who] refuses to waive immunity or to answer questions' extend Garrity beyond employees — the State may insist on answers only if it offers immunity from criminal use.

case_set.caption: Chavez v. Martinez
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: the privilege protects against being 'compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself' — Garrity-style compulsion becomes a completed violation only upon criminal use, cabining civil damages claims.

case_set.caption: Uniformed Sanitation Men Ass'n v. Commissioner of Sanitation
case_set.one_line_basis: Companion to Gardner: employees may not be fired for refusing to waive immunity, though they may be required to answer narrowly job-related questions under immunity; no lake record/cached text.

case_set.caption: Lefkowitz v. Cunningham
case_set.one_line_basis: Extends the line to political-party office; automatic penalties for invoking the privilege are unconstitutional compulsion; no lake record/cached text.

case_set.caption: Kastigar v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Use-and-derivative-use immunity is the constitutional measure of protection Garrity immunity mirrors (reaches the statement's fruits, per the registry statement); no lake record/cached text.

case_set.caption: Spevack v. Klein
case_set.one_line_basis: Companion to Garrity: disbarment may not be imposed for invoking the privilege; no lake record/cached text.

title: Brady and Giglio

case_set.caption: Mooney v. Holohan
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: a conviction procured 'through a deliberate deception of court and jury by the presentation of testimony known to be perjured' violates due process — the root of the disclosure duty.

case_set.caption: Napue v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: the State's failure to correct false testimony 'does not cease to apply merely because the false testimony goes only to the credibility of the witness.'

case_set.caption: Brady v. Maryland
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'the suppression by the prosecution of evidence favorable to an accused upon request violates due process where the evidence is material either to guilt or to punishment, irrespective of the good faith or bad faith of the prosecution.'

case_set.caption: Giglio v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: failure to disclose 'an alleged promise made to its key-witness that he would not be prosecuted' requires a new trial — 'nondisclosure of evidence affecting credibility' falls within Brady/Napue.

case_set.caption: United States v. Agurs
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: addresses 'the prosecutor['s]... obligation to provide defense counsel with exculpatory information when no request has been made' — the duty exists without a request, with materiality varying by situation.

case_set.caption: United States v. Bagley
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: adopts the Strickland-derived 'reasonable probability' materiality standard and treats impeachment evidence within the rule rather than under automatic reversal.

case_set.caption: Kyles v. Whitley
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: materiality 'turns on the cumulative effect of all such evidence suppressed,' and 'the individual prosecutor has a duty to learn of any favorable evidence known to the others acting on the government's behalf... including the police.'

case_set.caption: Strickler v. Greene
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'strictly speaking, there is never a real Brady violation' without materiality — articulating the three components (favorable evidence, suppression, prejudice).

case_set.caption: Banks v. Dretke
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'A rule thus declaring prosecutor may hide, defendant must seek, is not tenable' — undisclosed paid-informant status and coached testimony ground cause and prejudice.

case_set.caption: Cone v. Bell
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: withheld evidence of drug use bore on sentencing even if not guilt — remand to assess the suppressed evidence against the punishment-phase case (Brady reaches punishment materiality).

case_set.caption: Connick v. Thompson
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'whether a district attorney's office may be held liable under §1983 for failure to train based on a single Brady violation. We hold that it cannot' — deliberate-indifference limit on systemic remedies.

case_set.caption: Smith v. Cain
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: where 'the eyewitness's testimony was the only evidence linking Smith to the crime, and the eyewitness's undisclosed statements contradicted his testimony,' the statements 'were plainly material.'

case_set.caption: Wearry v. Cain
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: summary reversal of a 'state postconviction court's judgment' where undisclosed inmate statements 'cast doubt on [the key witness's] credibility' — cumulative impeachment materiality.

case_set.caption: Turner v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: applies the 'reasonable probability' standard on a cumulative record and finds the withheld evidence immaterial against the corroborated 'group attack' theory — a materiality-discipline data point.

case_set.caption: Benn v. Lambert
case_set.one_line_basis: Text (9th Cir.): habeas relief where the state decision unreasonably applied 'Brady v. Maryland' to suppressed impeachment and accident evidence — circuit-level application in the lake set.

case_set.caption: United States v. Ruiz
case_set.one_line_basis: Lake identity record exists (2002) but carries no opinion text: the Constitution does not require pre-guilty-plea disclosure of impeachment information; basis from lane knowledge.

case_set.caption: Arizona v. Youngblood
case_set.one_line_basis: Failure to preserve potentially useful evidence violates due process only on bad faith — the destruction branch adjoining Brady; no lake record/cached text.

case_set.caption: California v. Trombetta
case_set.one_line_basis: Destroyed-evidence due process requires apparent exculpatory value plus no comparable substitute; no lake record/cached text.

case_set.caption: Weatherford v. Bursey

title: Plain view & plain feel -- a seizure justification at the search threshold

case_set.caption: Harris v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: 'Objects falling in the plain view of an officer who has a right to be in the position to have that view are subject to seizure' (opinion 107625) -- the pre-Coolidge formulation.

case_set.caption: Coolidge v. New Hampshire
case_set.one_line_basis: Plurality's plain-view framework (including the inadvertence requirement later discarded); rejected the State's theory that the car 'might be seized... because it was in plain view' (opinion 108377).

case_set.caption: Arizona v. Hicks
case_set.one_line_basis: 'Moving some of the components' to read serial numbers was a new search requiring probable cause -- plain view tolerates no manipulation and requires PC, not reasonable suspicion (opinion 9430865).

case_set.caption: Horton v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: Inadvertence resolved: an 'essential predicate' of lawful arrival, plus 'two additional conditions' -- incriminating character 'immediately apparent' and a lawful right of access -- with inadvertent discovery not required (opinion 9432041).

case_set.caption: Minnesota v. Dickerson

case_set.caption: New York v. Class
case_set.one_line_basis: Reaching into the car 'to move papers obscuring the VIN' was a search even though the VIN itself is unprotected (opinion 9430353) -- physical relocation to obtain view is a search, echoing Hicks.

case_set.caption: Soldal v. Cook County
case_set.one_line_basis: 'Our plain view decisions make untenable' the notion that seizures require a privacy invasion; plain view is a seizure doctrine protecting possessory interests (opinion 112795) -- grounds the topic's placement at the seizure threshold.

case_set.caption: Bond v. United States

case_set.caption: United States v. Watson

case_set.caption: Draper v. United States

case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'unprovoked flight upon noticing the police' in a high-crime area supports RS; 'nervous, evasive behavior is a pertinent factor.'

case_set.caption: Navarette v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: reliable 911 report of being run off the road 'created reasonable suspicion of drunk driving' justifying the stop.

case_set.caption: Kansas v. Glover
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: stop justified when 'the registered owner has a revoked driver's license' absent information negating the owner-is-driver inference; officers make 'commonsense judgments and inferences about human behavior.'

case_set.caption: Adams v. Williams
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: tip from an informant 'known to him personally' who 'had provided him with information in the past' justified the forcible stop — a stronger case than an anonymous telephone tip.

case_set.caption: Brown v. Texas
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: seizure invalid where officers lacked 'reasonable, articulable suspicion that a crime had just been, was being, or was about to be committed'; balancing requires individualized suspicion.

case_set.caption: United States v. Hensley
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: RS that a person 'was involved in or is wanted in connection with a completed felony' supports a stop; objective reliance on a 'wanted flyer' suffices if its issuer had RS.

case_set.caption: Heien v. North Carolina
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: an 'objectively reasonable' mistake of law (single brake light) 'can nonetheless give rise to the reasonable suspicion necessary to uphold the seizure.'

case_set.caption: United States v. Brignoni-Ponce
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: roving-patrol stops require 'specific and articulable facts'; apparent 'Mexican ancestry alone' cannot furnish the founded suspicion.

case_set.caption: Sibron v. New York
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: mere association with 'known ... narcotics addicts' over eight hours gave no basis; the officer's thrust into the pocket was unsupported by any articulable suspicion of danger.

title: The Proof Ladder

case_set.caption: Terry v. Ohio
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: the bottom rungs — a 'hunch' authorizes nothing; 'specific reasonable inferences ... in light of his experience' unlock the stop-and-frisk power.

case_set.caption: Illinois v. Gates
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: the probable-cause rung — 'fair probability' judged on the totality; a 'practical, nontechnical conception.'

case_set.caption: Brinegar v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: orders the ladder — PC is 'more than bare suspicion' and 'less than evidence which would justify condemnation'; 'the standard of proof is accordingly correlative to what must be proved.'

case_set.caption: United States v. Sokolow
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: explicit rung comparison — RS is 'considerably less than proof of wrongdoing by a preponderance of the evidence' and 'obviously less demanding than that for probable cause.'

case_set.caption: Ornelas v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: both field standards are 'fluid concepts that take their substantive content from the particular contexts' — resisting fixed quanta; de novo review of the ultimate questions.

case_set.caption: United States v. Arvizu
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: totality governs the RS rung; no divide-and-conquer discounting of individually innocent facts.

case_set.caption: Kansas v. Glover
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: the RS inquiry 'falls considerably short of 51% accuracy' — the ladder's field rungs sit below preponderance.

case_set.caption: Texas v. Brown
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: PC 'does not demand any showing that such a belief be correct or more likely true than false' — even the PC rung sits below more-likely-than-not.

case_set.caption: District of Columbia v. Wesby
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: PC 'is not a high bar' — 'probability or substantial chance,' not an actual showing.

title: Standing to Challenge a Search

case_set.caption: Rakas v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'Fourth Amendment rights are personal rights that may not be asserted vicariously'; rejects the 'target' theory and the Jones 'legitimately on [the] premises' gloss; the inquiry merges into substantive REP.

case_set.caption: Alderman v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: rights 'may not be vicariously asserted' — suppression of overheard conversations runs only to those with a personal interest in the premises or conversations.

case_set.caption: Katz v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places' — the expectation framework that Rakas makes the measure of who may suppress.

case_set.caption: Jones v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'anyone legitimately on premises where a search occurs may challenge its legality' plus automatic standing for possessory offenses — the historical rules later dismantled.

case_set.caption: United States v. Salvucci
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'the automatic standing rule of Jones v. United States ... is therefore overruled'; possession of the seized good no longer substitutes for a privacy showing.

case_set.caption: Rawlings v. Kentucky
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: claimed ownership of drugs in a companion's purse did not establish 'a reasonable expectation of privacy in Cox's purse' — ownership of the item is not enough.

case_set.caption: Minnesota v. Carter
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: visitors 'essentially present for a business transaction ... only in the home a matter of hours' with no prior relationship lack the protected expectation an overnight guest has.

case_set.caption: Minnesota v. Olson
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'an overnight guest in a house had the sort of expectation of privacy that the Fourth Amendment protects' (as restated in Carter's quotation of Olson).

case_set.caption: Byrd v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'the mere fact that a driver in lawful possession or control of a rental car is not listed on the rental agreement' does not defeat a reasonable expectation of privacy.

case_set.caption: Brendlin v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: a passenger 'is seized and thus entitled to challenge the government's action' when a traffic stop occurs — the stop itself is a seizure of every occupant.

case_set.caption: United States v. Payner
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: courts may not use the 'inherent supervisory power' to suppress evidence obtained by deliberately violating a third party's rights — the standing limit holds even against bad-faith exploitation.

case_set.caption: Mancusi v. DeForte
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: standing turns on 'whether the area was one in which there was a reasonable expectation of freedom from governmental intrusion' — union official could challenge search of an office 'shared by DeForte and several other union officials.'

case_set.caption: Simmons v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'testimony given by a defendant to meet such [standing] requirements should not be admissible against him at trial on the question of guilt or innocence' — cures the self-incrimination dilemma.

case_set.caption: United States v. Padilla
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: rejects the Ninth Circuit's 'coconspirator exception' conferring an expectation of privacy from 'a supervisory role in the conspiracy or joint control' — conspiracy membership adds nothing to REP.

negative_notes: No surviving automatic standing (Salvucci) and no target theory (Rakas); 'standing' persists as vocabulary while the analysis is substantive REP.
Brendlin is grounded here only for the passenger's power to challenge the stop as a seizure of his own person, not for any REP in the searched car (registry notes it re-homed).
No SCOTUS holding in the cached corpus maps standing for digital/third-party records; Carpenter is a search holding, not a standing framework.

title: Fruits & Attenuation

case_set.caption: Wong Sun v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: the question is not 'but for' causation but whether evidence 'has been come at by exploitation of that illegality or instead by means sufficiently distinguishable to be purged of the primary taint.'

case_set.caption: Brown v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: attenuation weighs 'temporal proximity,' 'the presence of intervening circumstances,' and 'particularly, the purpose and flagrancy of the official misconduct'; Miranda warnings 'alone and per se' do not break the chain.

case_set.caption: Utah v. Strieff
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: discovery of 'a valid arrest warrant' during an unconstitutional stop is an intervening circumstance; suppression declined absent 'flagrant misconduct' under the Brown factors.

case_set.caption: Nardone v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: origin of the phrase — proof that a substantial portion of the case is 'a fruit of the poisonous tree'; yet the connection 'may have become so attenuated as to dissipate the taint.'

case_set.caption: Silverthorne Lumber Co. v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: illegally obtained knowledge 'shall not be used at all' — but facts 'gained from an independent source they may be proved like any others.'

case_set.caption: United States v. Ceccolini
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: refuses a per se rule for live witnesses but requires 'attenuation between Officer Biro's search and Hennessey's testimony' analysis — witness free will eases the finding of dissipation.

case_set.caption: New York v. Harris
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: statement made 'outside their premises where the police have probable cause' is not the fruit of the Payton violation.

case_set.caption: Taylor v. Alabama
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: confession suppressed 'as the fruit of an illegal arrest' unless 'intervening events break the causal connection ... so that the confession is sufficiently an act of free will to purge the primary taint.'

case_set.caption: Kaupp v. Texas
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: applies the Brown line to a confession following an unconsented 3 a.m. removal — warnings alone insufficient to purge.

case_set.caption: Dunaway v. New York
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: statements taken during 'custodial questioning on less than probable cause' analyzed under Brown — attenuation, not voluntariness alone, controls.

case_set.caption: Segura v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: information 'unrelated to the entry ... constituted an independent source for the evidence under Silverthorne' — taint analysis stops where the lawful line begins.

case_set.caption: Murray v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'so long as a later, lawful seizure is genuinely independent of an earlier, tainted one' the independent-source doctrine admits it (fuller treatment homed on the Independent Source page).

case_set.caption: Nix v. Williams
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: evidence that 'would ultimately or inevitably have been discovered' admissible on proof 'by a preponderance of the evidence' (homed on Inevitable Discovery page; boundary case here).

case_set.caption: Hudson v. Michigan
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'but-for causation can be too attenuated to justify exclusion,' and attenuation 'can occur ... when suppression would not serve the interest protected by the constitutional guarantee violated' (knock-and-announce).

case_set.caption: Oregon v. Elstad
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: a voluntary confession after an unwarned admission is not automatically 'fruit of the poisonous tree' under Wong Sun — the Miranda-fruits track diverges from Fourth Amendment taint.

case_set.caption: United States v. Patane
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: whether Miranda 'requires suppression of the physical fruits of the suspect's unwarned but voluntary statements' — no; the pistol comes in.

case_set.caption: Michigan v. Tucker
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: witness identity learned from unwarned questioning admissible — the Wong Sun fruits rule presupposes an actual constitutional infringement.

case_set.caption: United States v. Crews
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: in-court identification admissible where 'based upon independent recollection untainted by the intervening identifications' — the defendant's presence is not itself suppressible fruit.

case_set.caption: Immigration & Naturalization Service v. Lopez-Mendoza
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'The body or identity of a defendant or respondent ... is never itself suppressible as a fruit of an unlawful arrest.'

negative_notes: No cached text fixes a numeric temporal-proximity threshold; Brown expressly declines any 'talismanic' single-factor test.
The Miranda-fruits foils (Elstad/Patane/Tucker) mark the boundary: Wong Sun taint doctrine runs on constitutional violations, not prophylactic-rule violations.
Independent source and inevitable discovery are adjacent doctrines homed on their own page; carried here only as limiting boundary cases.

title: Exigent Circumstances — Destruction of Evidence

case_set.caption: Kentucky v. King
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: warrantless entry to prevent 'destruction of evidence' is a recognized exigency, and under the police-created exigency doctrine the exception applies 'when the police do not gain entry to premises by means of an actual or threatened violation of the Fourth Amendment.'

case_set.caption: Schmerber v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: officer 'might reasonably have believed that he was confronted with an emergency, in which the delay necessary to obtain a warrant... threatened the destruction of evidence' (BAC dissipation), making the warrantless blood draw an appropriate incident of arrest.

case_set.caption: Missouri v. McNeely
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'the natural dissipation of alcohol in the bloodstream does not' create a per se exigency; exigency must be assessed case by case on the totality, rejecting a categorical BAC rule.

case_set.caption: Mitchell v. Wisconsin
case_set.one_line_basis: Text (plurality): 'exigency exists when (1) BAC evidence is dissipating and (2) some other factor creates pressing health, safety, or law enforcement needs'; both are met for unconscious drivers, so Schmerber controls and a warrantless blood draw is lawful.

case_set.caption: Birchfield v. North Dakota
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: distinguishes 'warrantless breath tests incident to arrests for drunk driving' (permitted) from blood tests, channeling routine BAC collection away from case-by-case destruction-of-evidence exigency.

case_set.caption: Cupp v. Murphy
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: warrantless fingernail scrapings sustained where police had probable cause and evidence of strangulation under fingernails was readily destructible — the detainee's evanescent-evidence exposure justified the very limited search.

case_set.caption: Vale v. Louisiana
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'We decline to hold that an arrest on the street can provide its own "exigent circumstance" so as to justify a warrantless search of the arrestee's house' — no shown impracticability of getting a warrant, no destruction exigency.

case_set.caption: Welsh v. Wisconsin
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: exigency claims for home entry are weakest 'when the underlying offense for which there is probable cause to arrest is relatively minor'; gravity of the offense is an important factor in the exigent-circumstances calculus.

case_set.caption: Illinois v. McArthur
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: relying on Segura's stake-out assumption and Mincey's police-guard point, a brief, tailored restraint preventing the occupant from entering his home unaccompanied while police obtained a warrant was a reasonable seizure to prevent evidence destruction.

case_set.caption: Richards v. Wisconsin
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: rejects Wisconsin's blanket rule that felony drug warrants 'necessarily' carry exigent circumstances for no-knock entry; destruction-of-evidence risk must rest on case-specific reasonable suspicion.

case_set.caption: United States v. Santana
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: once Santana saw the police 'there was likewise a realistic expectation that any delay would result in destruction of evidence,' citing Vale — destruction risk reinforcing the hot-pursuit entry.

negative_notes: Formerly live splits are resolved at SCOTUS: King settled the lower courts' divergent police-created-exigency tests (lawful-conduct rule); McNeely rejected the categorical BAC-dissipation exigency; Mitchell (plurality) governs unconscious drivers.

No SCOTUS holding fixes a quantum for how 'imminent' destruction must be outside the BAC line; the standard remains totality-based probable cause plus objectively reasonable belief of imminent destruction.

title: Exigent Circumstances — Emergency Aid

case_set.caption: Brigham City v. Stuart
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: police may enter a home when they have 'an objectively reasonable basis for believing that an occupant is seriously injured or imminently threatened with such injury'; cert was granted 'in light of differences among state courts and the Courts of Appeals concerning the appropriate Fourth Amendment standard.'

case_set.caption: Michigan v. Fisher
case_set.one_line_basis: Text (per curiam): applying Brigham City's 'objectively reasonable basis' test to reverse suppression where an officer entered after seeing a bleeding, raging occupant — error to demand evidence of a serious, life-threatening injury.

case_set.caption: Mincey v. Arizona
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: rejects Arizona's 'murder scene exception' — the four-day search of the apartment was not justified by any emergency; emergency aid ends when the exigency that legitimated entry is over.

case_set.caption: Thompson v. Louisiana
case_set.one_line_basis: Text (per curiam): warrantless 'murder scene' search 'is in direct conflict with our opinion in Mincey' — homicide-scene status alone creates no exigency.

case_set.caption: Flippo v. West Virginia
case_set.one_line_basis: Text (per curiam): suppression wrongly denied on the ground police may thoroughly search 'any crime scene'; Mincey forecloses a crime-scene exception.

case_set.caption: Ryburn v. Huff
case_set.one_line_basis: Text (per curiam, qualified immunity): officers who entered after judging that violence was imminent acted on Brigham City's 'imminently threatened' branch given school-violence context; reasonable officers could believe entry lawful.

case_set.caption: Caniglia v. Strom
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'Neither the holding nor logic of Cady justifies such warrantless searches and seizures in the home' — the First Circuit's 'freestanding community-caretaking' extension is rejected; welfare rationales must fit the emergency-aid/exigency framework.

case_set.caption: Cady v. Dombrowski
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: caretaking search upheld because 'police-citizen contact involving automobiles' is constitutionally distinct from contact 'in a home or office' — the vehicle caretaking case emergency-aid claims must be distinguished from.

case_set.caption: Welsh v. Wisconsin

title: Entry to Arrest

case_set.caption: Payton v. New York
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: strikes NY statutes authorizing police 'to enter a private residence without a warrant and with force, if necessary, to make a routine felony arrest'; an arrest warrant founded on probable cause carries the limited authority to enter the suspect's own dwelling when there is reason to believe he is within.

case_set.caption: Steagald v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: an arrest warrant for a guest does not protect the third-party homeowner's privacy interest — Fourth Amendment rights 'are personal in nature'; entry into a third party's home to arrest requires a search warrant absent consent or exigency.

case_set.caption: United States v. Watson
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: warrantless public arrest on probable cause is the 'usual rule' (quoting Carroll) and constitutional — the public-place baseline against which the home-entry rule cuts.

case_set.caption: United States v. Santana
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: a suspect standing in her open doorway is in a 'public' place with no expectation of privacy, so Watson governs the arrest's initiation and hot pursuit justifies following her retreat inside.

case_set.caption: Minnesota v. Olson
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: an 'overnight guest' has a legitimate expectation of privacy in the host's home, and the warrantless entry to arrest him required exigency — approving the Minnesota standard (hot pursuit, destruction of evidence, danger) which was not met.

case_set.caption: New York v. Harris
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: where entry violated Payton but the arrest rested on probable cause, the station-house statement made outside the home is not suppressible — Payton protects the home, not a subsequent out-of-home statement.

case_set.caption: Welsh v. Wisconsin
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: warrantless home entry to arrest for a 'relatively minor' offense is presumptively unreasonable; gravity of the offense conditions any exigency-based entry to arrest.

case_set.caption: Lange v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: flight of a suspected misdemeanant 'does not always — that is, categorically — justify a warrantless' entry; case-by-case assessment governs entry to arrest a fleeing misdemeanant.

case_set.caption: Johnson v. United States (1948)
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: entry and arrest on opium odor invalid — 'No reason is offered for not obtaining a search warrant except the inconvenience to the officers'; convenience never justifies dispensing with a warrant at the threshold.

case_set.caption: United States v. Nora

title: Exigent Circumstances — Hot Pursuit

case_set.caption: Warden v. Hayden
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: warrantless entry and search for a just-fled armed robber valid because 'the exigencies of the situation made that course imperative' (quoting McDonald) — the fountainhead hot-pursuit entry.

case_set.caption: United States v. Santana
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'hot pursuit means some sort of a chase, but it need not be an extended hue and cry'; a pursuit beginning at the doorway and ending inside is a 'true hot pursuit' governed by Hayden.

case_set.caption: Welsh v. Wisconsin
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: gravity of the underlying offense is 'an important factor'; the presumption of unreasonableness for warrantless home entry is 'difficult to rebut' when the offense is minor (civil-forfeiture OWI).

case_set.caption: Lange v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'Courts are divided' on misdemeanor pursuit (citing Stanton v. Sims 'noting the split'); held — flight of a suspected misdemeanant does not categorically justify warrantless entry; case-by-case exigency required.

case_set.caption: Kentucky v. King
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: exigent-circumstances entry (including pursuit-adjacent destruction risk) is unavailable only where police 'gain entry by means of an actual or threatened violation of the Fourth Amendment' — the police-created-exigency limit on pursuit entries.

case_set.caption: Minnesota v. Olson
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: approves the standard requiring 'hot pursuit of a fleeing felon, or imminent destruction of evidence,' or danger to occupants, with the gravity of the crime weighed — and finds it unmet for a getaway driver already contained.

case_set.caption: Mincey v. Arizona
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: exigency justifying entry does not carry a continuing right to search; the four-day homicide-scene search 'was not justified by any emergency threatening life or limb' once the scene was secure.

case_set.caption: Johnson v. United States (1948)
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: no fleeing suspect, only officer 'inconvenience' — the case marking where pursuit-type urgency is absent and a warrant is required.

case_set.caption: Stanton v. Sims
case_set.one_line_basis: Cited in Lange's text as 'noting the split' on misdemeanor hot pursuit (571 U.S. 3, 6-7 (2013) (per curiam)); QI granted because the question was unsettled. No lake record or cached text.

case_set.caption: McDonald v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Quoted at length in Welsh (Jackson, J., concurring: exigency depends 'upon the gravity of the offense') and supplies Hayden's 'exigencies of the situation' formulation; no lake record or cached text.

title: Fire-Scene Entries

case_set.caption: Michigan v. Tyler
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'A burning building clearly presents an exigency of sufficient proportions to render a warrantless entry reasonable'; officials 'may remain there for a reasonable time to investigate the cause of the blaze,' and later entries require administrative-warrant procedures (citing Camara) or a criminal warrant.

case_set.caption: Michigan v. Clifford
case_set.one_line_basis: Text (plurality): where 'reasonable expectations of privacy remain' post-fire, re-entry requires a warrant whose type turns on 'the object of the search' — administrative for cause-and-origin, criminal on probable cause where the primary object is evidence of arson.

case_set.caption: Camara v. Municipal Court
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: administrative inspections of dwellings require warrant-procedure protection, with reasonableness assessed by 'balancing the need to search against the invasion which the search entails' — the framework Tyler imports for post-fire entries.

case_set.caption: See v. City of Seattle
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: extends Camara to commercial premises — warrantless code-enforcement inspection of a commercial warehouse cannot be compelled on pain of prosecution; supplies the commercial-structure branch for fire-scene doctrine.

case_set.caption: Mincey v. Arizona
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: no offense-scene exception — the emergency entry rationale expires with the emergency; the fire-scene 'reasonable time' allowance is the calibrated alternative Tyler builds against Mincey's backdrop.

case_set.caption: Olmstead v. United States

case_set.caption: Katz v. United States

case_set.caption: United States v. Jones

case_set.caption: Florida v. Jardines

case_set.caption: Grady v. North Carolina

case_set.one_line_basis: Officers with probable cause 'prevented that man from entering the home for about two hours while they obtained a search warrant' — a limited, tailored seizure of the premises held reasonable.

case_set.caption: Arizona v. Hicks
case_set.one_line_basis: The floor of 'meaningful interference': 'the mere recording of the serial numbers did not constitute a seizure' — information copying deprives the owner of nothing possessory (moving the equipment was instead a search).

case_set.caption: United States v. Karo
case_set.one_line_basis: Transfer of a beeper-laden can to an unwitting buyer was no seizure: 'it cannot be said that anyone's possessory interest was interfered with in a meaningful way' — a technical trespass without meaningful interference does not seize.

case_set.caption: United States v. James Daniel Good Real Property
case_set.one_line_basis: Seizure of real property for forfeiture: absent exigency, due process requires notice and a hearing before seizing real property — the seizure doctrine's intersection with forfeiture practice.

case_set.caption: United States v. $8,850 in Currency
case_set.one_line_basis: Post-seizure timing: the reasonableness of the government's delay between seizing currency and instituting forfeiture proceedings is tested by a Barker-style balancing; lake record has no cached opinion text — unverified.

negative_notes: No SCOTUS holding fixes a bright-line hour limit for detaining effects on reasonable suspicion — Place condemns 90 minutes on its facts while Van Leeuwen tolerates 29 hours for mail; the doctrine is diligence-based, not clock-based.
Seizure of the person is governed by a different formula (intent to restrain/submission, Hodari D./Torres) — the possessory-interference test is property-specific.
Torres v. Madrid was screened for a property-side contrast quote and none was found in its cached text; it stays on the person page.

title: When a Seizure Occurs

case_set.caption: Terry v. Ohio
case_set.one_line_basis: The root formulation: 'Only when the officer, by means of physical force or show of authority, has in some way restrained the liberty of a citizen may we conclude that a seizure has occurred.'

case_set.caption: United States v. Mendenhall
case_set.one_line_basis: The objective test: a person is seized 'only if, in view of all of the circumstances surrounding the incident, a reasonable person would have believed that he was not free to leave,' with examples (several officers, weapon display, touching, compelling tone).

case_set.caption: California v. Hodari D.
case_set.one_line_basis: The two branches fixed: 'the mere grasping or application of physical force with lawful authority, whether or not it succeeded in subduing the arrestee,' is a seizure; a show of authority seizes only upon submission — flight defeats it.

case_set.caption: Torres v. Madrid
case_set.one_line_basis: Force branch completed: 'The application of physical force to the body of a person with intent to restrain is a seizure even if the person does not submit and is not subdued' — police bullets that struck but did not stop Torres seized her.

case_set.caption: Michigan v. Chesternut
case_set.one_line_basis: Police pursuit alone is not a seizure: the patrol car's parallel 'chase' 'would not have communicated to a reasonable person that he was not at liberty to ignore the police presence and go about his business.'

case_set.caption: Brower v. County of Inyo
case_set.one_line_basis: Seizure requires 'a governmental termination of freedom of movement through means intentionally applied' — the roadblock the fleeing driver crashed into was such a means; an accidental stopping is not.

case_set.caption: Florida v. Bostick
case_set.one_line_basis: Where a person's freedom of movement is restricted by factors independent of police (a bus), the question becomes 'whether a reasonable person would feel free to decline the officers' requests or otherwise terminate the encounter.'

case_set.caption: United States v. Drayton
case_set.one_line_basis: Applies Bostick: officers may approach bus passengers at random and request consent 'provided a reasonable person would understand that he or she is free to refuse'; no per se warning requirement.

case_set.caption: Florida v. Royer
case_set.one_line_basis: Escalation point: an initially consensual airport encounter became an unlawful detention when officers kept Royer's ticket and license and moved him to a small room without probable cause — 'the entire encounter was consensual' was 'untenable.'

case_set.caption: INS v. Delgado
case_set.one_line_basis: Factory-survey questioning was no seizure of the workforce: brief questioning while agents were posted at exits did not restrain freedom of movement; not a lake record, but its own opinion text is cached and grounds this row.

case_set.caption: Brendlin v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: A traffic stop seizes the passenger as well as the driver — the passenger submits to a show of authority and may challenge the stop's constitutionality.

case_set.caption: Dunaway v. New York
case_set.one_line_basis: Custodial-transport line: taking a suspect to headquarters in a police car for interrogation is an arrest-level seizure requiring probable cause, whatever the label.

case_set.caption: Kaupp v. Texas
case_set.one_line_basis: Applying Dunaway: a 3 a.m. 'we need to go and talk,' handcuffing, and shoeless removal of a teenager from his home was an arrest; 'Okay' in those circumstances is not consent.

case_set.caption: Hayes v. Florida
case_set.one_line_basis: Transporting a suspect to the station house for fingerprinting 'without his consent and without probable cause or prior judicial authorization' crosses the line from Terry stop to arrest.

case_set.caption: Davis v. Mississippi
case_set.one_line_basis: Fingerprint-dragnet detentions were illegal seizures: investigatory detentions without probable cause are subject to the Fourth Amendment and their fruits excludable.

case_set.caption: County of Sacramento v. Lewis
case_set.one_line_basis: The no-seizure foil: a high-speed pursuit that ends in a fatal collision is not a Fourth Amendment seizure absent means intentionally applied to terminate movement; the claim sounds (if at all) in due process.

negative_notes: The two branches never merged: force seizures need no submission (Torres), show-of-authority seizures always do (Hodari D.) — no case applies a single unified test.

Duration/continuity of a force-based seizure is expressly left open in Torres's cached text ('a seizure is a single act, and not a continuous fact'): how long the Torres seizure lasts is undecided at SCOTUS.
Detention-incident-to-warrant cases (Summers/Bailey/Mena) were screened out as authority-to-detain doctrine rather than threshold when-a-seizure-occurs doctrine.

title: Stop-and-Identify

case_set.caption: Hiibel v. Sixth Judicial Dist. Court
case_set.one_line_basis: A state stop-and-identify statute requiring only that a suspect 'disclose his name' during a valid Terry stop violates neither the Fourth Amendment (the request related to the stop's circumstances) nor, on these facts, the Fifth.

case_set.caption: Kolender v. Lawson
case_set.one_line_basis: A statute demanding 'credible and reliable' identification from Terry-stopped persons is unconstitutionally vague — it vests complete enforcement discretion in the officer; the statutory instrument must itself be valid.

case_set.caption: Brown v. Texas
case_set.one_line_basis: The predicate rule: appellant 'refused to identify himself' but could not be punished because the officers lacked 'a reasonable suspicion, based on objective facts' — a stop-and-identify statute cannot operate without a valid stop.

case_set.caption: Terry v. Ohio
case_set.one_line_basis: The baseline dictum (White, J., concurring, in the cached cluster text): 'the person stopped is not obliged to answer, answers may not be compelled, and refusal to answer furnishes no basis for an arrest' — the default Hiibel's statute displaces only as to one's name.

case_set.caption: Berkemer v. McCarty
case_set.one_line_basis: Terry-stop questioning dictum: the officer may ask 'a moderate number of questions... But the detainee is not obliged to respond,' and absent probable cause he must be released — no free-standing duty to answer.

case_set.caption: Northrup v. City of Toledo Police Dept.
case_set.one_line_basis: Sixth Circuit application: where state law permits open carry, visibly carrying a holstered gun gives no reasonable suspicion to stop, disarm, and demand identification — the ID demand cannot bootstrap its own stop.

case_set.caption: United States v. Landeros
case_set.one_line_basis: Ninth Circuit: demanding identification from a passenger without independent reasonable suspicion unlawfully extends the stop (913 F.3d 862 (2019)); lake record has no cached opinion text — unverified.

negative_notes: Hiibel's Fifth Amendment holding is expressly case-bound: it reserves the situation where furnishing one's name would itself be incriminating.
No SCOTUS holding requires production of documentary ID during a Terry stop — Hiibel's cached text stresses the Nevada statute demands only that the suspect state his name.
No SCOTUS holding on ID demands to passengers during traffic stops; the Ninth Circuit's Landeros addresses it but is unverified here.
Absent a statute, refusal to identify remains non-arrestable under the Terry/Berkemer dicta — the duty is a creature of state law.

title: Terry Stops and Reasonable Suspicion

case_set.caption: Terry v. Ohio
case_set.one_line_basis: The charter: a brief stop on articulable suspicion plus a frisk where the officer reasonably believes the person 'armed and presently dangerous,' limited to 'a pat down of the outer clothing' for weapons.

case_set.caption: Sibron v. New York
case_set.one_line_basis: Companion boundary: thrusting a hand into Sibron's pocket exceeded Terry — no facts suggested a weapon and the search was for narcotics, not protection.

case_set.caption: Peters v. New York
case_set.one_line_basis: Companion upholding (same cluster as Sibron): the officer's observation of apparent burglary conduct justified the seizure and the discovery was sustained.

case_set.caption: Adams v. Williams
case_set.one_line_basis: A known informant's tip can supply reasonable suspicion, and the officer's reach to the exact spot indicated — the waistband — was a permissible protective response.

case_set.caption: United States v. Cortez
case_set.one_line_basis: The measuring rule: 'the totality of the circumstances — the whole picture — must be taken into account,' yielding 'a particularized and objective basis for suspecting the particular person stopped.'

case_set.caption: United States v. Sokolow
case_set.one_line_basis: The quantum: reasonable suspicion 'is considerably less than proof of wrongdoing by a preponderance of the evidence'; profile-consistent facts may still amount to suspicion in combination.

case_set.caption: Reid v. Georgia
case_set.one_line_basis: Foil to Sokolow: drug-courier-profile characteristics describing 'a very large category of presumably innocent travelers' are 'simply too slender a reed to support the seizure.'

case_set.caption: Alabama v. White
case_set.one_line_basis: Anonymous tip plus corroboration of predictive details sufficed — 'a close case' setting the floor for tip-based suspicion.

case_set.caption: Florida v. J.L.
case_set.one_line_basis: The other side of White: 'an anonymous tip that a person is carrying a gun is, without more,' insufficient — reliability requires predictive indicia, and there is no firearm exception.

case_set.caption: Navarette v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: A contemporaneous 911 report of being run off the road bore adequate indicia of reliability and 'created reasonable suspicion of drunk driving.'

case_set.caption: Illinois v. Wardlow
case_set.one_line_basis: 'Unprovoked flight upon noticing the police' in a high-crime area supports a stop; presence in such an area alone does not.

case_set.caption: United States v. Arvizu
case_set.one_line_basis: Totality review 'precludes this sort of divide-and-conquer analysis' — factors innocent in isolation may together create suspicion, with deference to officer inference.

case_set.caption: Kansas v. Glover
case_set.one_line_basis: The commonsense-inference case: a registered owner's revoked license supports stopping the vehicle absent information negating the owner-is-driver inference.

case_set.caption: United States v. Hensley
case_set.one_line_basis: Terry extends to completed felonies: officers may stop a person subject of a 'wanted flyer' in objective reliance on another department's reasonable suspicion.

case_set.caption: Florida v. Royer
case_set.one_line_basis: Scope discipline: 'The scope of the detention must be carefully tailored to its underlying justification' and employ 'the least intrusive means reasonably available.'

case_set.caption: United States v. Sharpe
case_set.one_line_basis: Duration has no bright line: ask 'whether the police diligently pursued a means of investigation that was likely to confirm or dispel their suspicions quickly' — 20 minutes upheld.

case_set.caption: Michigan v. Long
case_set.one_line_basis: Frisk extends to the car: a protective search of the passenger compartment, 'limited to those areas in which a weapon may be placed,' is permitted on suspicion the suspect is dangerous and may access a weapon.

case_set.caption: Minnesota v. Dickerson
case_set.one_line_basis: 'Plain feel' cabined: contraband identity must be 'immediately apparent' during the weapons pat-down — 'squeezing, sliding and otherwise manipulating' a pocket known to hold no weapon exceeds Terry.

case_set.caption: Ybarra v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: No companion or premises frisk: 'a person's mere propinquity to others independently suspected of criminal activity does not, without more,' justify search or frisk — suspicion must be individualized.

case_set.caption: United States v. Brignoni-Ponce
case_set.one_line_basis: Race/ancestry cannot carry the stop: 'Mexican ancestry alone' cannot support a roving-patrol founded suspicion; Terry-style balancing governs immigration stops.

case_set.caption: United States v. Rideau
case_set.one_line_basis: Fifth Circuit en banc illustration: nighttime, a high-crime area, apparent intoxication, and evasive backing-away made a protective pat-down reasonable — context legitimately amplifies danger.

case_set.caption: United States v. Vinton
case_set.one_line_basis: D.C. Circuit car-frisk application: a visible knife within reach during a traffic stop justified a Long protective search that included the locked briefcase in the passenger compartment.

case_set.caption: United States v. Robinson (4th Cir. en banc)
case_set.one_line_basis: En banc holding that a suspect reasonably believed armed during a lawful forced stop is thereby dangerous for frisk purposes, whether or not the carry may be legal (846 F.3d 694 (2017)); no cached text — unverified.

case_set.caption: United States v. Black
case_set.one_line_basis: Fourth Circuit: where firearm possession is lawful, possession alone gives no reasonable suspicion for the stop itself (707 F.3d 531 (2013)); no cached text — unverified.

case_set.caption: Northrup v. City of Toledo Police Dept.
case_set.one_line_basis: Sixth Circuit (verified text): lawful open carry, without more, creates no reasonable suspicion of criminality permitting a stop, disarmament, and handcuffing — 'Ohio law permits the open carry of firearms... and thus permitted Northrup to do exactly what he was doing.'

splits.question: Where gun possession may be lawful, is a detainee reasonably suspected of being armed automatically 'presently dangerous' for Terry-frisk purposes ('armed and dangerous' as one inference or two)?

positions.direction: armed implies dangerous during a lawful forced stop, even in a permit state (frisk stage)

positions.case: Northrup v. City of Toledo Police Dept., 785 F.3d 1128 (2015)
positions.direction: lawful open carry alone supplies no reasonable suspicion to stop, disarm, or handcuff
lawful possession alone cannot generate reasonable suspicion for the stop itself — reconciled with Robinson by the stop/frisk stage distinction

negative_notes: Terry's frisk power is weapons-only; no case authorizes an evidence frisk (Dickerson polices the line).
No SCOTUS holding resolves the armed-equals-dangerous question in legal-carry regimes — the split above is circuit-level only.
No SCOTUS bright-line maximum duration for a Terry stop (Sharpe expressly rejects one).
Sibron and Peters share cluster 107730 (decided together); rows are separate because their holdings cut opposite ways.

title: Traffic Stops

case_set.caption: Delaware v. Prouse
case_set.one_line_basis: Random, standardless spot checks are unreasonable: stopping a car requires 'at least articulable and reasonable suspicion' that the motorist is unlicensed, the car unregistered, or an occupant otherwise subject to seizure.

case_set.caption: Whren v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Objective justification controls: probable cause of any civil traffic violation validates the stop regardless of the officer's actual motivations — pretext arguments and 'reasonable officer would have' tests rejected.

case_set.caption: Heien v. North Carolina
case_set.one_line_basis: Reasonable suspicion can rest on an objectively reasonable mistake of law (the one-brake-light stop); the officer's subjective understanding is irrelevant.

case_set.caption: Rodriguez v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: The duration rule: a stop 'become[s] unlawful if it is prolonged beyond the time reasonably required to complete the mission of issuing a ticket' — no de minimis extension for a dog sniff without independent suspicion.

case_set.caption: Illinois v. Caballes
case_set.one_line_basis: A dog sniff performed during a lawful stop 'generally does not implicate legitimate privacy interests' — lawful if it does not extend the stop (the line Rodriguez enforces).

case_set.caption: Pennsylvania v. Mimms
case_set.one_line_basis: Officers may order the driver out of a lawfully stopped vehicle as a matter of course — the incremental intrusion is de minimis against officer safety.

case_set.caption: Maryland v. Wilson
case_set.one_line_basis: Mimms 'extends to passengers as well' — passengers may be ordered out of a lawfully stopped car.

case_set.caption: Arizona v. Johnson
case_set.one_line_basis: Passenger frisks on Terry grounds during stops; and 'inquiries into matters unrelated to the justification for the traffic stop do not convert the encounter' so long as they do not measurably extend it.

case_set.caption: Brendlin v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: The stop seizes 'everyone in the vehicle' — passengers have standing to challenge the stop.

case_set.caption: Berkemer v. McCarty
case_set.one_line_basis: The ordinary stop is 'presumptively temporary and brief,' 'more analogous to a so-called Terry stop... than to a formal arrest' — roadside questioning is not Miranda custody.

case_set.caption: Pennsylvania v. Bruder
case_set.one_line_basis: Per curiam reaffirming Berkemer for ordinary roadside stops and sobriety questioning.

case_set.caption: Ohio v. Robinette
case_set.one_line_basis: No 'free to go' advisement is required before a consent request after a completed stop — voluntariness is a totality question.

case_set.caption: Knowles v. Iowa
case_set.one_line_basis: No search incident to citation: issuing a ticket rather than arresting supplies neither rationale for a full vehicle search.

case_set.caption: Atwater v. City of Lago Vista
case_set.one_line_basis: Custodial arrest is permitted even for 'a minor criminal offense, such as a misdemeanor seatbelt violation punishable only by a fine' — traffic enforcement can escalate to arrest without a warrant.

case_set.caption: New York v. Class
case_set.one_line_basis: During a lawful stop an officer could move papers obscuring the dashboard VIN — no reasonable expectation of privacy in the federally mandated, publicly visible VIN.

case_set.caption: Kansas v. Glover
case_set.one_line_basis: Running a plate and learning the registered owner's license is revoked supports the stop absent information negating the owner-as-driver inference.

case_set.caption: Navarette v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: A reliable 911 tip of being run off the road created reasonable suspicion of drunk driving sufficient to stop the truck without personal observation of bad driving.

case_set.caption: Michigan Dept. of State Police v. Sitz
case_set.one_line_basis: Suspicionless sobriety checkpoints upheld under Brown v. Texas programmatic balancing — the highway-safety carve-out from Prouse's individualized-suspicion rule.

case_set.caption: City of Indianapolis v. Edmond
case_set.one_line_basis: Checkpoints 'whose primary purpose is the discovery and interdiction of illegal narcotics' are invalid — programs serving the general interest in crime control need individualized suspicion.

case_set.caption: Illinois v. Lidster
case_set.one_line_basis: Information-seeking checkpoints (asking motorists about a hit-and-run) are reasonable — Edmond does not govern stops seeking the public's help about others' crimes.

case_set.caption: United States v. Martinez-Fuerte
case_set.one_line_basis: Fixed immigration checkpoints with brief stops and secondary referrals are permissible without individualized suspicion — the fixed-checkpoint pillar behind Sitz/Lidster.

case_set.caption: United States v. Landeros
case_set.one_line_basis: Ninth Circuit: extending a stop to demand a passenger's identification without independent suspicion violates Rodriguez (913 F.3d 862 (2019)); no cached text — unverified.

negative_notes: No SCOTUS holding on whether officers may compel passenger identification during a routine stop — Hiibel involved a statute and a Terry stop; Landeros is circuit-level and unverified here.
Whren immunizes pretext only under the Fourth Amendment; its cached text preserves Equal Protection as the home for selective-enforcement claims.
