title: Inevitable Discovery & Independent Source

case_set.caption: Nix v. Williams
case_set.one_line_basis: Inevitable discovery: if the prosecution shows 'ultimately or inevitably would have been discovered by lawful means -- here the volunteers' search -- then the deterrence rationale has so little basis that the evidence should be received'; burden is 'preponderance of the evidence' (opinion 9429647).

case_set.caption: Murray v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Independent source applies where the later warrant is a 'genuinely independent source of the information and tangible evidence at issue' -- not if the decision to seek it was 'prompted by what they had seen during the initial entry' or the illegal observations affected the magistrate (opinion 9431434).

case_set.caption: Segura v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Evidence first seen during illegal entry admissible where warrant rested on an 'independent source' under 'Silverthorne Lumber Co.' -- information wholly unconnected to the entry (opinion 9429757).

case_set.caption: Silverthorne Lumber Co. v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Origin of the doctrine: facts 'gained from an independent source they may be proved like any others, but the knowledge gained by the Government's own wrong cannot be used by it' (opinion 99506).

case_set.caption: Wong Sun v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Baseline fruits framework both doctrines carve into: suppression turns on whether evidence came 'by exploitation of that illegality or instead by means sufficiently distinguishable to be purged of the primary taint' (opinion 106515).

case_set.caption: United States v. Crews
case_set.one_line_basis: Victim's 'in-court identification' need not be 'suppressed as the fruit of the defendant's unlawful' arrest; identity/independent-recollection not a suppressible fruit (opinion 9427838).

case_set.caption: Brewer v. Williams
case_set.one_line_basis: Predicate for Nix: detective 'deliberately and designedly set out to elicit information from Williams'; the body's location later saved via inevitable discovery on remand track (opinion 109624).

case_set.caption: Hudson v. Michigan
case_set.one_line_basis: Uses causation logic adjacent to these doctrines: 'Exclusion may not be premised on the mere fact' of a but-for chain -- interest-attenuation limits suppression even where discovery followed a violation (opinion 145646).

case_set.caption: United States v. Conner (8th Cir. 1997)
case_set.one_line_basis: 8th Cir. requires proof '(1) ... reasonable probability that the evidence would have been discovered by lawful means' and '(2) that the government was actively pursuing a substantial, alternative line of investigation at the time' (quoting 5th Cir. Wilson) (opinion 9490703).

case_set.caption: United States v. Lundin (9th Cir. 2016)
case_set.one_line_basis: 9th Cir.: 'The inevitable discovery exception does not apply when officers have probable cause to apply for a warrant but simply fail to do so' (citing Mejia, Echegoyen); also separates the two doctrines ('would have' vs. actually obtained) (opinion 3187625).

case_set.caption: United States v. Soto-Peguero (1st Cir. 2020)
case_set.one_line_basis: 1st Cir. permits the hypothetical-warrant route: government must establish 'the officers inevitably would have applied for a warrant, obtained it, and discovered the evidence' (Zapata/Procopio three-part framing) (opinion 4578375).

case_set.caption: United States v. Neugin (10th Cir. 2020)
case_set.one_line_basis: 10th Cir. rule set: preponderance that evidence 'would have been discovered in the absence of the Fourth Amendment violation,' provable via hypothetical lawful inventory (Ibarra), judged on 'demonstrated historical facts, not speculative elements' (opinion 4530911).

case_set.caption: United States v. Braxton (10th Cir. 2023)
case_set.one_line_basis: Applies the 10th Cir. 'counterfactual inquiry into what would have happened under lawful circumstances' (Souza line) and holds the doctrine inapplicable where the backpack's retention itself was invalid (opinion 9377330).

case_set.caption: United States v. Evans (10th Cir. 1991)
case_set.one_line_basis: Upholds search as lawful inventory and expressly declines to reach the district court's alternative inevitable-discovery holding -- illustrates the doctrine's role as fallback (opinion 564407).

case_set.caption: United States v. Gooch (9th Cir. 1993)
case_set.one_line_basis: Applies Murray's allocation: 'it is the function of the District Court rather than the Court of Appeals to determine the facts' underlying an independent-source claim (opinion 654273).

case_set.caption: United States v. August (5th Cir. 2025)
case_set.one_line_basis: Recent 5th Cir. application: magazine clip 'alternatively admissible under the independent source' doctrine where the warrant decision was not prompted by, and its affidavit not tainted by, the challenged entry (opinion 11041510).

positions.direction: No -- doctrine inapplicable when officers had probable cause to apply for a warrant but simply failed to do so
Yes -- government may prove officers inevitably would have applied for, obtained, and executed the warrant

positions.case: United States v. Conner (adopting 5th Cir. Wilson)
positions.direction: Only with an active-pursuit limit: government must have been actively pursuing a substantial alternative line of investigation at the time of the violation

positions.case: United States v. Neugin / Souza / Braxton
positions.direction: Permissive counterfactual 'would have' inquiry (including hypothetical inventory), but confined to demonstrated historical facts, not speculation

splits.confidence: high

negative_notes: No SCOTUS holding resolves the hypothetical-warrant / active-pursuit division; Nix itself involved an actual ongoing volunteer search.
Nix rejects a bad-faith exception ('police did not act in bad faith' inquiry raised and holding does not require good faith) -- burden is preponderance only.

title: The Good-Faith Exception

case_set.caption: United States v. Leon
case_set.one_line_basis: Suppression of evidence 'obtained in objectively reasonable reliance on a subsequently invalidated search warrant cannot justify the substantial costs' of exclusion; four failure situations in text: 'knowing or reckless falsity,' magistrate who 'abandoned his judicial role,' affidavit 'so lacking in indicia of probable cause,' facially deficient warrant (opinion 9429766).

case_set.caption: Massachusetts v. Sheppard
case_set.one_line_basis: Companion: no suppression where officers 'reasonably believed that the search they conducted was authorized by a valid warrant' despite the judge's failure to fix the form (opinion 111263).

case_set.caption: Illinois v. Krull
case_set.one_line_basis: Extends Leon to statutes: 'objectively reasonable reliance on a statute would have as little deterrent effect on the officer's actions' as reliance on a warrant (opinion 111835).

case_set.caption: Arizona v. Evans
case_set.one_line_basis: Extends to 'clerical errors of court employees' -- record errors by court staff do not trigger exclusion aimed at police (opinion 9433091).

case_set.caption: Herring v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Culpability threshold: 'To trigger the exclusionary rule, police conduct must be sufficiently deliberate that exclusion can meaningfully deter it'; 'isolated negligence attenuated from the search' (negligent police recordkeeping) does not qualify (opinion 145922).

case_set.caption: Davis v. United States, 564 U.S. 229 (2011)
case_set.one_line_basis: Good faith for searches conducted in objectively reasonable reliance on binding appellate precedent -- CAUTION: the lake record's cached text (opinion 7268220) is a cert-denial stub, not the 564 U.S. 229 opinion; basis grounded indirectly via 9th Cir. Cano quoting 'Davis, 564 U.S. at 232' (opinion 4426344).

case_set.caption: Groh v. Ramirez
case_set.one_line_basis: The facially-deficient floor: 'warrant was so obviously deficient that we must regard the search as "warrantless"' -- no objectively reasonable reliance on a warrant lacking particularity (opinion 131161).

case_set.caption: Franks v. Delaware
case_set.one_line_basis: The false-affidavit floor Leon preserves: suppression where affidavit rests on 'deliberate falsehood or ... reckless disregard for the truth,' on a substantial preliminary showing (opinion 109925).

case_set.caption: Malley v. Briggs
case_set.one_line_basis: Civil analog of the same objective standard: officer must have an 'objectively reasonable basis for believing that the facts alleged in his affidavit are sufficient to establish probable cause' (opinion 9430379).

case_set.caption: Messerschmidt v. Millender
case_set.one_line_basis: Qualified-immunity application of warrant reliance: the 'shield of immunity' is lost only in the rare case where the warrant is so lacking that official belief in its existence is unreasonable (opinion 623242).

case_set.caption: Michigan v. DeFillippo
case_set.one_line_basis: Pre-Krull antecedent: arrest under a 'presumptively valid ordinance is valid regardless of whether the ordinance subsequently is declared unconstitutional' (opinion 110127).

case_set.caption: United States v. Smith (5th Cir. 2024)
case_set.one_line_basis: Holds 'geofence warrants -- at least as described' unconstitutional yet applies good faith '[g]iven the novelty and complexity of geofence warrants, as well as the dearth of legal authority,' distinguishing Groh as 'run-of-the-mill' (opinion 10502720).

case_set.caption: United States v. Morton (5th Cir. 2022, en banc)
case_set.one_line_basis: '[L]aw enforcement is usually entitled to rely on warrants'; good faith sustains broad-category cell-phone warrant searches under circuit precedent (opinion 7803054).

case_set.caption: United States v. Cano (9th Cir. 2019)
case_set.one_line_basis: Narrow Davis reading: good faith 'applies only to searches where binding appellate precedent ... specifically authorizes the police's search' (quoting Lara); rejected for forensic border phone search (opinion 4426344).

case_set.caption: United States v. Jackson (8th Cir. 2015)
case_set.one_line_basis: Standard Leon application: warrant application 'failed to supply probable cause,' yet 'the Leon good faith exception ... allowed the admission of evidence'; affirmed (opinion 2798587).

case_set.caption: United States v. Chatrie (4th Cir. en banc, 136 F.4th 100)
case_set.one_line_basis: Geofence good-faith litigation counterpart to Smith; lake carries the record but NO cached opinion text for either the en banc opinion or the 2026 SCOTUS docket -- cannot text-ground its position.

title: The Exclusionary Rule

case_set.caption: Weeks v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Letters seized 'in direct violation of the constitutional rights of the defendant' who 'made a seasonable application for' their return could not be retained and used -- the federal exclusion rule's birth (opinion 98094).

case_set.caption: Wolf v. Colorado
case_set.one_line_basis: Declined to impose exclusion on the states: 'we must hesitate to treat this remedy as an essential ingredient of the right'; later overruled on that point (opinion 104709).

case_set.caption: Mapp v. Ohio
case_set.one_line_basis: '[A]ll evidence obtained by searches and seizures in violation of the Constitution is, by that same authority, inadmissible in a state court' -- extends exclusion to the states, overruling Wolf (opinion 106285).

case_set.caption: Elkins v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Abolishes the 'silver platter doctrine': state-obtained evidence that would violate the Fourth Amendment if federally obtained is inadmissible in federal trials (opinion 9422064).

case_set.caption: United States v. Calandra
case_set.one_line_basis: The modern characterization: a 'judicially created remedy designed to safeguard Fourth Amendment rights generally through its deterrent effect, rather than a personal' right; no application to grand jury questioning (opinion 108898).

case_set.caption: United States v. Janis
case_set.one_line_basis: No exclusion in a federal 'civil proceeding': the deterrent gain 'surely does not outweigh the cost to society of extending' the rule there (opinion 109539).

case_set.caption: INS v. Lopez-Mendoza
case_set.one_line_basis: No exclusion in civil 'deportation proceeding[s]' -- BIA position sustained on cost-benefit balancing (opinion 9429772).

case_set.caption: Pennsylvania Bd. of Probation and Parole v. Scott
case_set.one_line_basis: No exclusion at 'parole revocation hearings' -- the rule does not follow the evidence into state administrative revocation (opinion 9433685).

case_set.caption: Walder v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Illegally obtained evidence may be used for 'impeaching the defendant's credibility' when he opens the door -- first impeachment carve-out (opinion 105188).

case_set.caption: United States v. Havens
case_set.one_line_basis: Suppressed evidence may 'impeach a defendant's false trial testimony, given in response to proper cross-examination' (opinion 9427937).

case_set.caption: James v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: The carve-out stops at the defendant: impeachment use against 'defense witnesses other than the defendant himself' is NOT permitted (opinion 112350).

case_set.caption: Hudson v. Michigan
case_set.one_line_basis: Interest-served causation limit: for a 'knock-and-announce violation, the only issue is whether the exclusionary rule' applies, and 'Exclusion may not be premised on the mere fact' of but-for causation -- no suppression (opinion 145646).

case_set.caption: Herring v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: States the governing cost-benefit trigger for the whole modern rule: 'To trigger the exclusionary rule, police conduct must be sufficiently deliberate that exclusion can meaningfully deter it' (opinion 145922).

case_set.caption: Stone v. Powell
case_set.one_line_basis: Federal habeas limit on relitigating Fourth Amendment suppression claims after a full and fair state opportunity -- NOT a lake record; no cached text to ground it.

negative_notes: No SCOTUS holding extends exclusion beyond the criminal case-in-chief: Janis (civil tax), Lopez-Mendoza (deportation), Scott (parole revocation) and Calandra (grand jury) all refuse it.

title: Lineups & the Right to Counsel

case_set.caption: United States v. Wade
case_set.one_line_basis: Post-indictment lineup is among the 'critical stages at which the accused has the right to the presence of his counsel'; in-court identification then requires an 'independent origin'/'independent source' showing (opinion 9423472).

case_set.caption: Gilbert v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: Testimony that a witness identified the accused at the uncounseled lineup is subject to a 'per se exclusionary rule ... an effective sanction to assure that law enforcement authorities will' respect the right (opinion 107487).

case_set.caption: Kirby v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: No counsel right before 'initiation of adversary judicial criminal proceedings -- whether by way of formal charge, preliminary hearing, indictment, information, or arraignment' (opinion 108554).

case_set.caption: United States v. Ash
case_set.one_line_basis: No counsel right at a 'photographic display, containing a picture of the accused, for the purpose of allowing a witness to attempt an identification' -- the accused is not present, so no trial-like confrontation (opinion 108846).

case_set.caption: Stovall v. Denno
case_set.one_line_basis: The parallel due-process track: a confrontation 'unnecessarily suggestive and conducive to irreparable mistaken identification' denies due process, judged on 'the totality of the circumstances' (opinion 107488).

case_set.caption: Manson v. Brathwaite
case_set.one_line_basis: Due-process track's test: 'reliability is the linchpin in determining the admissibility of identification testimony for both pre- and post-' Stovall confrontations (opinion 109693).

case_set.caption: Perry v. New Hampshire
case_set.one_line_basis: Due-process screening applies only to suggestive circumstances 'arranged by law enforcement officers' -- no 'improper law enforcement activity,' no preliminary judicial inquiry (opinion 7268276).

case_set.caption: Moore v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: Applies Wade/Gilbert to a one-on-one identification at a preliminary hearing (post-attachment, corporeal, accused present) -- NOT a lake record; no cached text to ground it.

negative_notes: No SCOTUS case extends the counsel right to any pre-attachment identification procedure (Kirby) or to any procedure at which the accused is not physically present (Ash).
Moore v. Illinois absent from the lake -- the preliminary-hearing showup application is unverifiable from cache.

The due-process cases (Stovall/Brathwaite/Perry) are the multi-homed Eyewitness Identification node's anchors (fairtrial.eyewitness also_on this page) -- included here as foils marking the doctrinal boundary.

title: Sixth Amendment Right to Counsel

case_set.caption: Massiah v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Incriminating words 'deliberately elicited from him after he had been indicted and in the absence of his retained counsel' cannot be used -- the foundational rule (opinion 106822).

case_set.caption: Kirby v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: Attachment line: the right begins at 'initiation of adversary judicial criminal proceedings -- whether by way of formal charge, preliminary hearing, indictment, information, or arraignment' (opinion 108554).

case_set.caption: Rothgery v. Gillespie County
case_set.one_line_basis: Attachment occurs at the 'initial appearance before a magistrate' -- with or without a prosecutor's involvement (opinion 145785).

case_set.caption: United States v. Gouveia
case_set.one_line_basis: No attachment for inmates held in 'administrative segregation ... before any adversary judicial proceedings had been initiated against them' (opinion 9429629).

case_set.caption: Brewer v. Williams
case_set.one_line_basis: '[J]udicial proceedings had been initiated against Williams before the start of the automobile ride'; detective 'deliberately and designedly set out to elicit information' -- violation without formal interrogation (opinion 109624).

case_set.caption: United States v. Henry
case_set.one_line_basis: Paid jailhouse informant 'deliberately elicited' statements within Massiah's meaning -- government-created situation likely to induce incrimination (opinion 9427972).

case_set.caption: Kuhlmann v. Wilson
case_set.one_line_basis: The 'listening post' limit: defendant must show 'some action, beyond merely listening, that was designed deliberately to elicit incriminating remarks' (opinion 9430620).

case_set.caption: Maine v. Moulton
case_set.one_line_basis: State may not 'knowingly circumvent[] the accused's right to have counsel present in a confrontation between the accused and a state agent' -- applies even in a meeting the defendant initiated (opinion 9430241).

case_set.caption: Michigan v. Jackson
case_set.one_line_basis: Treated post-arraignment 'assertion of the right to counsel [as] a significant event' barring police-initiated waiver -- expressly overruled by Montejo (opinions 9430407, 145873).

case_set.caption: Montejo v. Louisiana
case_set.one_line_basis: 'Michigan v. Jackson should be and now is overruled' -- attachment plus counsel-request no longer bars police-initiated, Miranda-waived approaches (opinion 145873).

case_set.caption: McNeil v. Wisconsin
case_set.one_line_basis: The right is 'offense specific' -- invoking it at arraignment on one charge does not bar questioning on uncharged matters (opinion 9432329).

case_set.caption: Texas v. Cobb
case_set.one_line_basis: Offense-specificity measured by the Blockburger 'same offense' test -- closely related factual conduct is not enough (opinion 9434063).

case_set.caption: Patterson v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: Post-indictment questioning valid where the accused went through the Miranda 'waiver procedure ... reading petitioner his rights, having petitioner initial each one, and sign a waiver form' -- Miranda warnings suffice for Sixth Amendment waiver (opinion 9431404).

case_set.caption: Fellers v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: The Sixth Amendment standard is whether officers 'deliberately elicited' the statements -- distinct from Fifth Amendment custodial interrogation; fruits question remanded (opinion 131158).

case_set.caption: Moran v. Burbine
case_set.one_line_basis: The 'right to counsel does not attach until after the initiation of formal charges' -- pre-charge station-house events (and the attorney's exclusion) do not implicate it (opinion 111614).

case_set.caption: Escobedo v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: Focus-of-investigation trigger ('the investigation is no longer a general inquiry into an unsolved crime but has begun to focus on a particular suspect') -- superseded as a Sixth Amendment rule by Kirby's attachment line (opinions 106883, 108554).

case_set.caption: Spano v. New York
case_set.one_line_basis: Pre-Massiah due-process route: post-indictment confession condemned on voluntariness grounds ('involuntary confessions does not turn alone on their inherent untrustworthiness') -- the doctrinal predecessor (opinion 105917).

case_set.caption: Edwards v. Arizona
case_set.one_line_basis: The Fifth Amendment analog the offense-specific cases contrast: suspect 'having expressed his desire to deal with the police only through counsel, is not subject to further interrogation ... until counsel has been made available' (opinion 9428324).

case_set.caption: Kansas v. Ventris
case_set.one_line_basis: Statements taken in violation of Massiah admissible for impeachment -- NOT a lake record; no cached text to ground it.

negative_notes: No split derived from the cached texts: the major internal disagreement (Jackson) was resolved by outright overruling in Montejo, not by a live division.
Kansas v. Ventris (impeachment use) and Johnson v. Zerbst (classic waiver standard) are absent from the lake; Ventris carried as candidate_unverified, Zerbst omitted.
No SCOTUS holding attaches the right earlier than initiation of adversary judicial proceedings -- arrest and focus-of-suspicion theories (Escobedo) are dead letters after Kirby/Gouveia/Burbine.

title: Detention and Search of Persons at the Scene

case_set.caption: Michigan v. Summers
case_set.one_line_basis: '[A] warrant to search for contraband founded on probable cause implicitly carries with it the limited authority to detain the occupants' while the search proceeds (opinion 9428436).

case_set.caption: Muehler v. Mena
case_set.one_line_basis: Detention in 'handcuffs during a search of the premises' was reasonable, and questioning about 'immigration status during the detention' was no 'independent Fourth Amendment violation' (opinion 142878).

case_set.caption: Bailey v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Summers authority is spatially confined to 'the immediate vicinity of the premises covered by a search warrant' -- an occupant stopped nearly a mile away is outside it (opinion 9502775).

case_set.caption: Ybarra v. Illinois
case_set.one_line_basis: No search of persons merely present: 'a person's mere propinquity to others independently suspected of criminal activity does not, without more, give rise to probable cause to search that person' (opinion 9427721).

case_set.caption: Los Angeles County v. Rettele
case_set.one_line_basis: Manner-of-detention bound: orders holding residents (even 'out of bed naked ... at gunpoint') during a valid search were 'permissible, and perhaps necessary, to protect the safety of the deputies' on those facts (opinion 145728).

case_set.caption: Illinois v. McArthur
case_set.one_line_basis: Adjacent securing-the-scene power: police could reasonably prevent the occupant 'from entering the trailer unaccompanied' while a warrant was obtained -- the pre-warrant analog of Summers (opinion 118405).

negative_notes: No SCOTUS case authorizes a full search (as opposed to detention) of a person found on the premises absent cause particularized to that person (Ybarra); the warrant's authority runs to the place, not the visitors.
Bailey's own line-drawing (immediate vicinity) is stated categorically in the cached text; no post-Bailey SCOTUS refinement appears in the lake.

title: Knock-and-Announce

case_set.caption: Wilson v. Arkansas
case_set.one_line_basis: The 'common-law knock and announce principle forms a part of the Fourth Amendment reasonableness inquiry' -- announcement is constitutionally grounded but not absolute (opinion 117936).

case_set.caption: Richards v. Wisconsin
case_set.one_line_basis: No-knock entry requires 'reasonable suspicion that knocking and announcing their presence, under the particular circumstances, would be dangerous or futile, or that it would inhibit the effective investigation'; rejects a 'blanket exception ... for this entire category of criminal activity' (felony drug cases) (opinion 118103).

case_set.caption: United States v. Ramirez
case_set.one_line_basis: Whether officers may make a 'no-knock entry' does not 'depend[] on whether property is damaged in the course of the entry' -- no heightened standard for destructive entries (opinion 118180).

case_set.caption: United States v. Banks
case_set.one_line_basis: '15 to 20 seconds' after knocking without response sufficed before forcible entry where destruction of drug evidence was the exigency -- timing judged by the exigency, not occupant convenience (opinion 131146).

case_set.caption: Hudson v. Michigan
case_set.one_line_basis: Remedy stripped: for a 'knock-and-announce violation, the only issue is whether the exclusionary rule' applies -- it does not; civil suits and internal discipline are the remedies (opinion 145646).

case_set.caption: Sabbath v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Statutory (18 U.S.C. § 3109) side: an 'unannounced intrusion into a dwelling -- what § 3109 basically proscribes' -- includes opening a closed but unlocked door; 'breaking' is not limited to physical destruction (opinion 107718).

case_set.caption: Miller v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: The pre-Wilson § 3109 announcement foundation (arrest entry invalid absent notice of authority and purpose) -- NOT a lake record; no cached text to ground it.

negative_notes: No SCOTUS authority permits ANY categorical (offense-type) no-knock exception -- Richards is emphatic; the showing is case-specific reasonable suspicion.
After Hudson, no cached SCOTUS text supports suppression as a knock-and-announce remedy; the doctrine's enforcement now runs through § 1983 and § 3109 contexts.
Miller v. United States (1958) absent from the lake; Ker v. California likewise absent -- the state-side historical strand is unverifiable from cache.

title: Scope Manner and Related Issues

case_set.caption: Dalia v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: A warrant need not specify how it will be executed ('covert entry' to plant a bug upheld); 'the manner in which a warrant is executed is subject to later judicial review as to its reasonableness' (opinion 110061).

case_set.caption: Sgro v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Warrant life/staleness: 'the proof must be of facts so closely related to the time of the issue of the warrant as to justify a finding of probable cause' -- a lapsed warrant cannot simply be redated (opinion 101970).

case_set.caption: Zurcher v. Stanford Daily
case_set.one_line_basis: A '"third party" search' is valid on probable cause that evidence is on the premises -- rejecting the claim that non-suspect 'third parties [may be reached] only by subpoena, not by search warrant' (opinion 109876).

case_set.caption: Winston v. Lee
case_set.one_line_basis: Manner can be unreasonable even with authorization: compelled 'surgical procedure under a general anesthetic for removal of a bullet' too intrusive on these facts (opinion 9429963).

case_set.caption: Wilson v. Layne
case_set.one_line_basis: '[I]t is a violation of the Fourth Amendment for police to bring members of the media or other third parties into a home during the execution of a warrant when the presence of the third parties' does not aid the warrant's execution -- the media ride-along rule (opinion 9433801).

case_set.caption: Hanlon v. Berger
case_set.one_line_basis: Companion applying Layne where a 'media crew recorded the officers' conduct in executing the warrant' at a ranch (opinion 1087699).

case_set.caption: Maryland v. Garrison
case_set.one_line_basis: Reasonable-mistake execution rule: search of the wrong 'third floor apartment' valid where officers reasonably believed the floor held one unit and desisted on discovering the error (opinion 9430836).

case_set.caption: Arizona v. Hicks
case_set.one_line_basis: Actions 'unrelated to the objectives of the authorized intrusion, which exposed to view concealed portions of the apartment or its contents' (moving stereo equipment) are a separate search needing their own justification (opinion 9430865).

case_set.caption: Horton v. California
case_set.one_line_basis: Seizure of items discovered while executing a warrant: 'inadvertence is a characteristic of most legitimate plain-view seizures,' but 'it is not a necessary condition' (opinion 9432041).

case_set.caption: United States v. Ramirez
case_set.one_line_basis: Property destruction during entry does not raise the constitutional bar for the entry itself, though 'destruction of property in their execution of the warrant' remains reviewable for reasonableness (opinion 118180).

negative_notes: No SCOTUS case invalidates a warrant for failing to prescribe its manner of execution (Dalia) -- manner is policed ex post under reasonableness.
Zurcher's third-party-premises rule has no cached SCOTUS retrenchment; statutory accommodations (Privacy Protection Act) are outside the cache and not asserted.
Media-presence liability was prospective only in Layne (qualified immunity granted there) -- the rule binds executions after 1999.

title: Section 1983 & Municipal Liability

case_set.caption: Monroe v. Pape
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: Section 1983 reaches those 'who, under color of any statute, ordinance, regulation, custom, or usage, of any State' deprive federal rights -- a remedy 'against those who representing a State in some capacity were unable or unwilling to enforce a state law', i.e., misuse of state authority is actionable without exhausting state remedies.

case_set.caption: Monell v. Department of Social Services
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'a municipality cannot be held liable under Section 1983 on a respondeat superior theory'; liability lies where the unconstitutional action 'implements or executes a policy statement, ordinance, regulation, or decision officially adopted and promulgated by that body's officers'.

case_set.caption: Screws v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: quoting Classic, 'Misuse of power, possessed by virtue of state law and made possible only because the wrongdoer is clothed with the authority of state law, is action taken under color of state law' -- the under-color definition Monroe imports into 1983.

case_set.caption: City of Canton v. Harris
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: 'We hold today that the inadequacy of police training may serve as the basis for Section 1983 liability only where the failure to train amounts to deliberate indifference to the rights of persons with whom the police come into contact.'

case_set.caption: Pembaur v. City of Cincinnati
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: a single decision can be municipal policy, but 'liability attaches only where the decisionmaker possesses final authority to establish municipal policy with respect to the action ordered'.

case_set.caption: Connick v. Thompson
case_set.one_line_basis: Text: rejects 'single-incident' failure-to-train liability hypothesized in Canton where the policymaker was not 'aware of a pattern of similar' violations (Brady-training claim fails).

case_set.caption: City of St. Louis v. Praprotnik
case_set.one_line_basis: Not cached in lake; identification of the final policymaker is a question of state law -- refinement of Pembaur's final-authority rule.

case_set.caption: Board of County Commissioners of Bryan County v. Brown
case_set.one_line_basis: Not cached in lake; single hiring decision requires rigorous causation -- plainly obvious consequence -- before municipal liability attaches.

case_set.caption: Owen v. City of Independence
case_set.one_line_basis: Not cached in lake; municipalities enjoy no good-faith/qualified immunity from 1983 damages.

case_set.caption: Will v. Michigan Department of State Police
case_set.one_line_basis: Not cached in lake; a State (and state officials sued in official capacity for damages) is not a 'person' under 1983.

case_set.caption: Kentucky v. Graham
case_set.one_line_basis: Not cached in lake; official-capacity suits are suits against the entity, personal-capacity suits against the officer -- the capacity framework the municipal-liability rules presuppose.

case_set.caption: Hafer v. Melo
case_set.one_line_basis: Not cached in lake; state officials sued in their personal capacities are 'persons' answerable in damages under 1983.

case_set.caption: West v. Atkins
case_set.one_line_basis: Not cached in lake; a private party performing a state function (contract physician) acts under color of state law.

case_set.caption: Heck v. Humphrey
case_set.one_line_basis: Not cached in lake; favorable-termination bar -- no 1983 damages claim that would necessarily imply the invalidity of an outstanding conviction.

title: Particularity

case_set.caption: Steele v. United States
case_set.one_line_basis: Text 100621: place description suffices where the officer can 'with reasonable effort ascertain and identify the place intended.'

case_set.one_line_basis: Text 106964: warrant for writings of the Communist Party condemned — 'The indiscriminate sweep of that language is constitutionally intolerable'; general-warrant/writs-of-assistance history grounds the rule, with First Amendment materials demanding the most scrupulous exactitude.

case_set.caption: Groh v. Ramirez
case_set.one_line_basis: Text 131161: 'the Fourth Amendment by its terms requires particularity in the warrant, not in the supporting documents'; a warrant that 'did not describe the items to be seized at all' was 'plainly invalid' and no detailed affidavit could cure it.

case_set.caption: Maryland v. Garrison
case_set.one_line_basis: Text 9430836: 'validity of the warrant must be assessed on the basis of the information that the officers disclosed, or had a duty to discover and to disclose, to the issuing Magistrate'; an objectively reasonable mistake about the number of third-floor apartments did not void the warrant or search.

case_set.caption: Andresen v. Maryland
case_set.one_line_basis: Text 109522: the catch-all phrase 'together with other fruits, instrumentalities and evidence of crime' was 'read as authorizing only the search for and seizure of evidence relating to the crime of false pretenses with respect to Lot 13T' — context can save an appended general phrase.

case_set.caption: Lo-Ji Sales, Inc. v. New York
case_set.one_line_basis: Text 110100: 'the search began and progressed pursuant to the sweeping open-ended authorization in the warrant' — an open-ended warrant to be filled in during execution is the general warrant the Amendment forbids.

case_set.caption: Zurcher v. Stanford Daily
case_set.one_line_basis: Text 109876: third-party premises may be searched on probable cause that evidence is there; the warrant machinery (probable cause, specificity of place/things) is what protects the innocent possessor.

case_set.caption: United States v. Grubbs
case_set.one_line_basis: Text 145670: the 'particularity requirement does not include the conditions precedent to an anticipatory search warrant' — only the two matters the text names (place; persons/things) must be particularly described in the warrant.

case_set.caption: Berger v. New York
case_set.one_line_basis: Text 9423459: New York's eavesdrop statute failed particularity — it authorized interception 'without requiring belief that any particular offense has been or is being committed' and without particularly describing the conversations to be seized.

case_set.caption: Messerschmidt v. Millender
case_set.one_line_basis: Text 623242: on the remedy side, officers relying on an arguably overbroad warrant keep qualified immunity unless 'plainly incompetent' in concluding the warrant was supported — reliance-immunity cabins particularity's damages bite.
